questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with swelling around his eyes, ankles, and abdomen, along with frothy urine. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine, and BUN levels. Image of renal biopsy is given below. Which of the following is not an established cause of this condition?

explanation.text: Based on the given clinical scenario and HPE image (segmental sclerosis, glomerular hyalinosis, and tubular atrophy, with negative immunofluorescence), the most likely diagnosis is Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults.

Diabetes mellitus primarily causes diabetic nephropathy, characterised by diffuse glomerulosclerosis rather than the focal and segmental pattern seen in FSGS. Causes of FSGS: 1. Primary (Idiopathic) FSGS. 2. Secondary FSGS: Mnemonic- H3R3S1 Hypertension (Option C) H IV associated nephropathy (Option B) H eroine drug abuse Reflux nephropathy R enal tissue loss S ickle cell anaemia (Option D) 3.
Inherited forms: Genetic mutations affecting slit diaphragm proteins like nephrin, podocin, α-actinin 4, and TRPC6.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy presents with sudden generalised oedema and frothy urine. Urinalysis reveals heavy proteinuria without hematuria. Renal biopsy widespread effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?

options.A: Lipid deposition within glomerular capillaries (tubular cells)
options.B: Immunofluorescence microscopy reveals granular deposition of IgG and C3 in the glomeruli.

explanation.text: The clinical and electron microscope findings suggest the diagnosis as Minimal Change Disease (MCD), characterised by diffuse effacement of foot processes of podocytes in glomeruli. It primarily affects children aged 2-6 years. MCD typically responds rapidly to corticosteroid therapy, especially in children (>90%), leading to complete remission of proteinuria and resolution of symptoms.

**Lipid deposition within glomerular capillaries (Option A):** Lipid deposition within glomerular capillaries is not observed in MCD. Instead, protein and lipid deposition may occur in the proximal tubules due to tubular reabsorption of lipoproteins passing through diseased glomeruli, leading to the historical term "lipoid nephrosis" for this disease.

**Immunofluorescence microscopy reveals granular deposition of IgG and C3 in the glomeruli (Option B):** Immunofluorescence studies in MCD typically show no significant immune complex deposition or granular staining patterns. This distinguishes MCD from immune complex-mediated glomerular diseases like IgA nephropathy or lupus nephritis, where IgG and C3 deposits are commonly observed.

**Non-selective proteinuria (Option D):** Minimal Change Disease (MCD) typically presents with highly selective proteinuria, mostly albumin. Renal function remains good despite massive proteinuria, with no hypertension or hematuria commonly.

questions.question: A 7-year-old girl with a recent upper respiratory tract infection presents with generalised swelling and reduced urine output. Urinalysis reveals proteinuria without blood cells or casts. Electron microscopy findings show flattening, retraction, and swelling of podocytes. Which light microscopy findings is characteristic of this condition?

explanation.text: The above clinical presentation and EM finding of podocyte effacement is characteristic of Minimal change disease. It is marked by the widespread flattening of podocytes, seen only on electron microscopy, while light microscopy shows normal glomeruli with lipids in proximal tubules.
This alteration in podocyte structure leads to increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier, resulting in the loss of large amounts of protein in the urine.

**Glomerulosclerosis (Option A):** Observed in diabetic nephropathy. Diffuse glomerulosclerosis Diffuse glomerulosclerosis Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Fibrinoid necrosis in the glomeruli (Option C) Vasculitis or immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis.
**Wire looping of capillaries (Option D):** Wire looping of capillaries is seen in diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, often due to SLE (lupus nephritis).

questions.question: A 36-year-old woman presents with intermittent flank pain and occasional gross hematuria. Physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory tests show normal renal function. A renal biopsy of a mass lesion reveals a mixture of mature adipose tissue, thick-walled blood vessels, and bundles of smooth muscle cells. All are true regarding this condition except?

options.A: It is commonly associated with tuberous sclerosis.
options.B: It is more prevalent in males than females.
options.C: It is mostly a benign tumor.
options.D: It has a high susceptibility to spontaneous hemorrhage.

explanation.text: Renal angiomyolipoma: A benign neoplasm consisting of vessels, smooth muscle, and fat originating from perivascular epithelioid cells. (Option C) It is most often detected incidentally and has a female preponderance. (Option B) They are present in 25% to 50% of patients with tuberous sclerosis. (Option A) It has a high susceptibility for bleeding (can present as loin pain).
Morphology: Histology: Circular blood vessels, muscles, and fat; perivascular epithelioid cells with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and mitotic figures.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy presents with complaints of blurred vision, hearing loss, and recurrent episodes of hematuria. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in Type 4 collagen. Which of the following genetic mutations is observed in the patient?

explanation.text: Mutations in COL4A3, COL4A4, COL4A5 genes are seen in Alport syndrome. Alport syndrome is caused by defective COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 genes, which lead to impaired production and deposition of the Type 4 collagen α345 chain network in the basement membranes of the glomerulus, cochlea, and eyes. It is predominantly inherited as an X-linked dominant trait. It has a triad of symptoms.
Blurred vision due to Anterior lenticonus, lens dislocation, posterior cataracts, and corneal dystrophy. Recurrent hematuria can lead to renal failure. Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.question: A 32-year-old male presents with painless hematuria post-upper respiratory infections, normal vital signs, and no oedema. Urinalysis reveals red blood cell casts and further investigation shows elevated serum creatinine and mild proteinuria. Renal biopsy confirms glomerulonephritis. What is the most common type of glomerulonephritis in this case?

explanation.text: IgA nephropathy, or Berger’s disease, is the most common type of glomerulonephritis in adults and worldwide. It presents with gross hematuria in adults, usually 2-3 days after an upper respiratory infection. It can progress to acute renal failure, causing ankle oedema, facial puffiness, and hypertension. It occurs due to the formation of aberrant IgA molecules that deposit in the mesangial regions.

**Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (Option B):** It is the most common type of glomerulonephritis in children and presents with fever, oliguria, hypertension, periorbital oedema, and hematuria. It usually occurs 1 to 2 weeks after recovery from an upper respiratory infection, which causes an inflammatory response (type III hypersensitivity reaction).
**Minimal change disease (Option C):** It is the most common type of nephrotic syndrome in children. It presents with massive proteinuria(>3.5g/24hrs) due to immunological damage to epithelial cells.

**Membranous nephropathy (Option D):** It is the most common type of nephrotic syndrome in the elderly. It is immune complex-mediated and can be caused by malignancy(colon, lung, melanoma), infections(malaria, hepatitis B, C, syphilis, schistosomiasis), drugs(gold, penicillamine), or autoimmune conditions(SLE).

questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with recurrent hematuria following upper respiratory infections and intermittent proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence and electron-dense deposits in the mesangium on electron microscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The clinical and histopathological findings suggest the diagnosis of Berger’s disease or IgA nephropathy, characterised by the deposition of IgA antibodies in the mesangial regions of the glomeruli, leading to recurrent episodes of hematuria. Electron microscopy reveals electron-dense deposits predominantly localised in the mesangium.

The characteristic immunofluorescent picture shows mesangial deposition of IgA, often with C3 and properdin and lesser amounts of IgG or IgM. Alport syndrome (Option B) It is a genetic disorder characterised by abnormalities in type IV collagen, leading to progressive kidney disease, hearing loss, and eye abnormalities. Electron microscopy reveals irregular thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with lamellation and splitting.
**Membranous nephropathy (Option C):** It is caused by the deposition of immune complexes (primarily IgG and C3) on the outer (subepithelial) side of the glomerular basement membrane.

**Buerger's Disease (Option D):** It is also called Thromboangiitis obliterans, it is a vascular disease causing extremity ischemia and is unrelated to renal involvement or immune deposits in the kidney. It does not present with hematuria or proteinuria.

questions.question: A 30-year-old male presents with increasing shortness of breath and hemoptysis. Lab tests show elevated serum creatinine and hematuria. Renal biopsy reveals linear immunofluorescence along the glomerular basement membrane and subepithelial and intramembranous electron-dense deposits on electron microscopy. Which of the following statements regarding the diagnosis is not true?

options.A: It is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction
options.B: Defective α3 chain of collagen IV
options.C: Linear immunofluorescence is due to IgG deposition
options.D: The most common cause of death is uremia.

explanation.text: Above mentioned scenario is a case of Goodpasture Syndrome It can be learnt as 1, 2, 3, 4 It is RPGN type 1 It is hypersensitivity type II and 4. Caused due to antibiotics against alpha 3 chain of type IV collagen. Immunofluorescence shows linear deposit of IgG and C3. (Picture below) Electron microscopy shows rupture and wrinkling of the basement membrane. Clinical Features: Lung involvement- haemoptysis, Renal involvement- haematuria.
Most common cause of death: Uremia.

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy presents with a recent sore throat, dark urine, fatigue, eye puffiness, and mild limb swelling. Urinalysis reveals hematuria, proteinuria, and red blood cell casts. Serum creatinine levels are slightly elevated. A renal biopsy shows the immunofluorescence image provided below. Which condition is not typically associated with this pattern of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis?

explanation.text: The clinical scenario indicates post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), a Type 2 RPGN (Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis) associated with granular immunofluorescence. Wegener's granulomatosis is Type 3 RPGN, characterised by pauci-immune glomerulonephritis with no immune deposits.

Type I RPGN (Anti-GBM antibody-mediated) Type II RPGN (Immune complex-mediated) Type III RPGN (Pauci-immune) (M/C type) Includes: Idiopathic Goodpasture syndrome Includes: Idiopathic Postinfectious glomerulonephritis Lupus (SLE) nephritis Henoch-Schönlein purpura IgA nephropathy Includes: ANCA-associated Idiopathic Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis ) Microscopic polyangiitis IF finding: Linear/ribbon pattern (Linear GBM deposits of IgG and C3) IF finding: Lumpy Bumpy/ Granular/ Starry Sky/Garland Pattern (granular antibody deposits) IF finding: No deposits Electron microscopy: R PGN causes R upture and w R inkling of GBM

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman with a history of SLE presents with fatigue, decreased urine output, and facial swelling. Lab tests show elevated serum creatinine, proteinuria, and hematuria. A renal biopsy is performed, and the histopathological examination image is attached. Which statement is true regarding this condition?

options.A: >50% of glomeruli showing crescents is diagnostic.
options.B: More the number of crescents, better the prognosis.
options.C: Crescents are composed solely of endothelial cells.

explanation.text: The provided clinical scenario and the histopathological image suggest a Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN) diagnosis in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Crescentic glomerulonephritis (or RPGN) is characterised by the presence of crescents in more than 50% of glomeruli on renal biopsy.

**More the number of crescents, the better the prognosis (Option B):** In RPGN, more crescents generally indicate a poor prognosis Crescents are composed solely of endothelial cells (Option C) Crescents are composed of fibrin, leucocytes, parietal and visceral layers of Bowman capsule.
**Primarily caused by bacterial infections (Option D):** RPGN Type I, II, III can be due to varied causes.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy presents with dark-coloured urine and puffiness around his eyes following a recent sore throat and skin infection. Laboratory tests show elevated serum creatinine, hematuria, and proteinuria. Renal biopsy image is given below. Which condition is most likely associated with these findings?

explanation.text: Pathological findings in PSGN Grossly Kidneys appear speckled or mottled due to numerous small haemorrhages (Flea-bitten appearance). Light microscopy Hypercellular glomeruli are caused by infiltration by leukocytes (neutrophils and monocytes) and the proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells.

Electron microscope ‘Subepithelial electron-dense humps’ due to immune complex deposition beneath the epithelial cells of the glomerular basement membrane. Immunofluorescence Characteristic 'Starry sky appearance' by immune complex deposition. Image showing Flea-bitten appearance Image showing Starry sky appearance Electron microscopy Incorrect options

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with complaints of frothy urine, as shown below, and severe generalised oedema. On physical examination, there is marked swelling in the legs and abdomen. Laboratory tests reveal significant proteinuria (3+ on dipstick) and hypoalbuminemia. Which of the following findings can be typically observed in this patient?

options.C: Red cell casts in the urine

explanation.text: Feature Nephritic Syndrome Nephrotic Syndrome Primary Characteristic Inflammation of glomeruli Increased permeability of glomerular basement membrane Proteinuria Mild to moderate (< 1 g/day) Severe (> 3.5 g/day) Hematuria Present (visible blood in urine or microscopic hematuria) Absent or very minimal Edema Mild, usually in the face and eyes Severe, generalised (anasarca) Blood Pressure Elevated (Hypertension) (Option D) Normal or slightly elevated Serum Albumin Slightly decreased or normal Markedly decreased (hypoalbuminemia) Lipid Levels Normal or slightly elevated Hyperlipidemia (Option B) Renal Function Often reduced (Azotemia) (Option A) Usually normal or slightly impaired Urine findings Red cell casts (Option C), granular casts Fatty casts, oval fat bodies & Maltese cross appearance (lipiduria) Common Causes Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis IgA nephropathy Minimal change disease Membranous nephropathy Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Symptoms Oliguria, hematuria (cola-colour urine), hypertension, thrombotic events (Loss of AT III via urine) Frothy urine, severe oedema

questions.question: A 65-year-old diabetic male presented to the hospital complaining of chronic abdominal discomfort and unexplained weight loss over the past few months. A palpable firm mass was detected on the left upper quadrant upon physical examination. Ultrasound revealed a large mass in the left upper pole of the kidney. Due to suspicion of renal malignancy, the patient underwent a left nephrectomy. Based on the specimen obtained, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Renal Oncocytoma: It is most commonly seen in > 50-year-old adults. It arises from the intercalated cells of the collecting ducts. Gross appearance: Tan or mahogany brown, with a central scar. Microscopy: Composed of pink eosinophilic cells with small, round, benign-appearing nuclei.

Electron microscope: Numerous mitochondria (granular appearance) Epithelioid angiomyolipoma (Option B) is a rare variant of angiomyolipoma composed of smooth muscle cells, fat, and blood vessels, and it often occurs in patients with tuberous sclerosis. However, the gross appearance of the specimen, without fat and showing a well-circumscribed mass, is more consistent with renal oncocytoma.

**Clear cell carcinoma (Option C):** would typically present with more aggressive features like hematuria, anemia, and vascular invasion. This patient's presentation along with a well-circumscribed mass is more typical of a benign tumor.

**Urothelial carcinoma (Option D):** is unlikely because the mass is located in the renal parenchyma, and in urothelial carcinoma it is typically found in the renal pelvis or ureter, often with associated hematuria.

questions.question: A child presents with hematuria and fever for the past 4 months. On examination, a mass-like structure was felt at the right flank. Which of the following features is not associated with this condition?

explanation.text: The given clinical vignette of a child with fever, hematuria, and abdominal mass in the right flank is suggestive of Wilm’s tumour or nephroblastoma. Bilateral malar and mandibular hypoplasia are characteristic of Treacher-Collins syndrome (not Wilms tumour). Syndromes associated with Wilm’s tumour are: Mutation Syndrome Features WT1 WAGR syndrome Wilms tumour.
**Aniridia (absent iris) (Option B):** .
**Genital anomalies (like cryptorchidism) (Option B):** . Intellectual disability.
**Denys-Drash syndrome Gonadal dysgenesis (male pseudohermaphroditism) (Option A):** .
**Early-onset nephropathy (leading to renal failure) (Option A):** . WT2 Beckwith-Widemann syndrome Organomegaly.
**Macroglossia (Option D):** . Hemihypertrophy. Omphalocele.
**Abnormal large cells in the adrenal cortex (adrenal cytomegaly) (Option D):** .

questions.question: A renal biopsy specimen has to be examined under microscopy for the presence of nephroblastoma. Presence of which of the following findings is less likely suggestive of the same?

explanation.text: Neuropils are eosinophilic fibrillary material surrounded by concentric groups of tumour cells ( Homer-Wright pseudorosettes ) seen in the histopathological examination of neuroblastoma. They are not seen in Wilm’s tumour. Characteristics Wilms Tumor Neuroblastoma Location Kidney Most common abdominal tumor in childhood Common site: adrenal medulla, Also seen in abdomen, pelvis & neck. Most common primary renal tumor in childhood.
Histological features Blastemal: Small blue cells. (Option B ruled out) Epithelial: Abortive tubules/glomeruli.

Stromal: Fibroblastic or myxoid. (Option D ruled out) Small blue cells with neuroblasts, neurofibrils (neuropils) (Option A), and mature ganglion cells Pseudo-rosettes (arrangements of small, round neuroblastic cells around a central fibrillary core) Histological image Below are the other components that might also be found in histological features of Wilm’s tumour: Squamous or mucinous epithelium. Smooth muscle.

**Adipose tissue (Option C ruled out):** . Cartilage. Osteoid. Neurogenic tissue. It is important to remember that around 5% of nephroblastoma is anaplastic, characterised by cells with large, hyperchromatic, pleomorphic nuclei and abnormal mitoses. TP53 mutation is associated with anaplasia.

questions.question: A histopathological report of renal biopsy done on a child states, “tumour cells suggestive of nephroblastoma along with adjacent sclerotic rests”. What is the risk associated with the presence of such sclerotic rests?

explanation.text: Nephrogenic rests are precursor or preneoplastic lesions of Wilms tumours, seen in the renal parenchyma adjacent to approximately. Hence, It is important to document the presence of nephrogenic rests in the resected specimen because these patients are at an increased risk of developing Wilms tumours in the contralateral kidney and require frequent and regular surveillance for many years.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding renal cell carcinoma is false?

options.A: Clear cell RCC is the most common type overall.
options.B: Papillary RCC is most commonly associated with dialysis patients.
options.C: Medullary RCC is commonly seen in sickle cell trait patients.
options.D: Papillary RCC has the best prognosis.

explanation.text: RCC subtype with the best prognosis is chromophobe RCC, which tends to grow slowly and is less likely to spread. Renal cell carcinoma: Age group Most common in the 6th and 7th decades. Male: Female ratio 2:1 Site of origin Proximal convoluted tubule. Risk factors Cigarette smoking (most important). Obesity (particularly in women) and hypertension. Unopposed estrogen therapy. Exposure to asbestos, petroleum products, and heavy metals.

End-stage renal disease. Chronic kidney disease. Acquired cystic disease. Tuberous sclerosis. Classification Sporadic: Most common type. Hereditary: Autosomal dominant, young age affected. Von-Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Hereditary leiomyomatosis & renal cell cancer syndrome. Hereditary papillary carcinoma. Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. Histological classification: Clear cell carcinoma (most common type) (Option A ruled out).
**Papillary cell carcinoma (associated with dialysis patients) (Option B ruled out):** .
**Chromophobe carcinoma (best prognosis) (Option D):** . Bellini duct (collecting duct) carcinoma. Xp11 translocation carcinoma.
**Medullary carcinoma (seen in patients with sickle cell trait) (Option C ruled out):** .

questions.question: A 45-year-old female died within a few months after being diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma. The autopsy revealed a yellowish, spherical neoplasm in one pole of the kidney. The tumour cells invaded the renal vein and inferior vena cava. Histopathology is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The clinical scenario and the histopathology image is suggestive of Clear cell carcinoma Clear cell carcinoma: Gross: The yellow colour results from the prominent lipid accumulations in tumour cells. It has a characteristic tendency to invade the renal vein, which may grow as a solid column of cells that extends up the inferior vena cava, sometimes as far as the right side of the heart.
Histopathology:. The tumour cells have cytoplasm containing glycogen and lipids.

questions.question: Hobnail nuclei are seen in which type of renal cell carcinoma?

explanation.text: Hobnail nuclei are a characteristic feature of collecting duct carcinoma/ Bellini duct carcinoma.
**Papillary renal cell carcinoma (Option B):** comprises cuboidal or low columnar cells arranged in papillary formations. Psammoma bodies may be present.
**Chromophobe renal carcinoma (Option C):** is made up of pale eosinophilic cells, often with a perinuclear halo, known as Plant.
